intro: Vallombrosa, in the mountains of Reggello above Florence, keeps its big trees in an arboretum started in 1869 so forestry students could experiment with trees from other parts of the world. Two of them are on Italy's national register: a giant sequoia 6.55 metres round and a Lambert pine the register puts at 51.5 metres tall. A short walk up the road stands the Holy Beech, heir to the tree of a legend from 1036, and deeper in the Sant'Antonio forest a twin-trunked beech has a walking loop named after it.
meta_description: Four monumental trees at Vallombrosa near Florence: a giant sequoia, a 51.5-metre Lambert pine, the Holy Beech and the Faggione of Sant'Antonio.
question_meta: What are the monumental trees of Vallombrosa?
question_answer: Vallombrosa has four trees on Italy's national register: a giant sequoia and a Lambert pine inside the experimental arboretum, the Holy Beech beside its chapel near the abbey, and the Faggione in the Sant'Antonio forest. The two arboretum trees are seen only on free guided visits, daily from June to September; the two beeches are on open forest roads and trails.
question_context: Vallombrosa is a day trip rather than a walk from Florence, about an hour and a quarter by train to Pontassieve and bus 343 up the mountain. What brings people is the abbey and the forest around it, and the trees are part of both. The arboretum was founded in 1869 for the Royal Forestry Institute and moved to its present ground in 1884, and it now holds around 5,000 specimens of more than 700 species. Only two of its trees are on the national register. The giant sequoia stands at the Belvedere delle sequoie among much younger relatives, and the Lambert pine, nicknamed Nazareno, is the one every source measures differently, between 40 and 54 metres. Neither has a published planting date. The Holy Beech is the only tree here with a sourced age: Reggello's tourism office calls it a shoot of the legendary original, about 150 years old, and a trail listing says 120. The Faggione, about 5 metres round and formed from two shoots grown together, stands about 3 kilometres east on the Anello del Faggione and is realistically reached by car. The arboretum cannot be entered unguided, so check the visit times before you travel.

faq.q: Can I visit the Vallombrosa arboretum on my own?
faq.a: No. The arboretum is seen on free guided visits of about 90 minutes, daily from June to September and on request the rest of the year, from beneath the abbey's Torrione.

faq.q: How do I get to Vallombrosa from Florence?
faq.a: Take the train from Santa Maria Novella to Pontassieve, then Autolinee Toscane bus 343 up to Vallombrosa. Allow about an hour and a quarter and check the timetable.

A beech beside the Cappella del Faggio Santo, said to be a shoot of the tree under which Giovanni Gualberto, founder of Vallombrosa, sheltered in March 1036. The standing tree is about 120 to 150 years old.

faq.q: How tall is the Lambert pine?
faq.a: The national register gives 51.5 metres. A guide on a 2023 visit said 54 and a botanical guide says over 40, so the exact figure is disputed.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Vallombrosa Arboretum

location.address: Arboreti sperimentali di Vallombrosa, Via del Paradisino, Vallombrosa, Reggello (FI)

trees.story:
Vallombrosa's arboretum began in 1869 as a classroom. Students of the Royal Forestry Institute planted trees from other parts of the world on this mountain to experiment with them, and the collection now holds around 5,000 specimens of more than 700 species, which a local visit report calls the largest plant collection of its kind in Italy.

Of all of them, only two are on Italy's national register of monumental trees, and this giant sequoia is one. The register measures it at 6.55 metres round and 36.5 metres tall, at 954 metres above sea level. An older, undated botanical guide gives it about 7.2 metres round. It stands at the Belvedere delle sequoie, among younger sequoias that a guide on a 2023 visit described as very young, so the old trunk is easy to pick out.

When was it planted? No source says. The arboretum was founded in 1869 and moved to its present ground in 1884, but nothing ties this tree to either date, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us.

A visitor recorded it standing in May 2026. You can only reach it on a free guided visit of about 90 minutes, led by Carabinieri biodiversity staff, daily from June to September and on request the rest of the year. The other registered tree, a Lambert pine, is on the same tour.
trees.access: Guided visits only, free, about 90 minutes: daily June to September (Monday to Saturday 10:30 and 14:00, Sundays and holidays 11:00 and 15:00) from beneath the abbey's Torrione; groups of ten or more book ahead. The rest of the year on request (by phone, +39 055 862020). Times from 2026 reports; check before going.
trees.transport: A day trip from Florence: train from Santa Maria Novella to Pontassieve, then Autolinee Toscane bus 343 to Vallombrosa (45 to 60 minutes on the bus, about an hour and a quarter door to door; check the timetable).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.55 metres round, far stouter than the young sequoias around it, with a low wooden rail ringing its base. It stands at the Belvedere delle sequoie on the guided route.
trees.pin_source: iNaturalist observation 375589030, 2026-05-24, GPS accuracy 10 m at 43.73282, 11.55631; the observer's note says the tree is on the monumental list with a 650 cm girth (2016 data), matching MASAF 06. Same spot as the Commons 'Sequoia gigante, Arboreto di Vallombrosa' geotag and the register point (within a few metres).
trees.verify_notes: Alive: iNaturalist observation 2026-05-24 at this spot. Existence: MASAF register 06/H222/FI/09 (girth 655 cm, height 36.5 m; observer's note on iNaturalist cites 650 cm, 2016 data) plus Visit Tuscany (Reggello comune tourism office) naming 'a Giant Redwood' as one of the two monumental trees of the arboreta, plus the Italian Botanical Heritage page listing a Sequoiadendron giganteum with a circumference of 23.62 ft (about 720 cm, older undated figure; conflicts with 655 cm, keep the register figure). No source dates this specimen: the arboretum was founded 1869 elsewhere or 1884 on the current site, but no source says this tree belongs to a particular planting, so age is left empty. Valdarno Post (2023, guided visit) calls the sequoias at the Belvedere 'giovanissime' with remarkable measures. Single iNaturalist photo set is all rights reserved: no use. Access is guided only, said plainly. Pin confirmed by the 10 m GPS observation, casual grade on iNaturalist.

trees.name: The Lambert Pine of the Vallombrosa Arboretum

location.address: Arboreti sperimentali di Vallombrosa, Via del Paradisino, Vallombrosa, Reggello (FI)

trees.story:
Nobody agrees how tall this pine is, and every figure is enormous. Italy's national register gives 51.5 metres. A guide on a 2023 visit told the group 54. An English-language botanical guide says over 40. The girths disagree as well, from the register's 5.15 metres to the guide's spoken almost 8, and whichever number you trust, the guide who leads visitors calls it the most imposing tree in the Vallombrosa arboretum.

It is a Lambert pine, also called the sugar pine, a North American species growing here in an arboretum founded in 1869 so forestry students could experiment with trees from other parts of the world. Nobody has published when this one went in. The same guide said its species grows the second-largest pine cone in the world, and the tour shows visitors one of them.

Locally it has a name, Nazareno. Tuscany's tourism site mentions the nickname and does not say where it came from. If you know, tell us that too.

It is one of only two trees inside the arboretum on the national monumental register; the other is the giant sequoia at the Belvedere a short walk away. Photographs from 2019 and 2021 show it standing, and the 2023 tour described it. You can see it only on a free guided visit of about 90 minutes, daily from June to September and on request the rest of the year.
trees.access: Guided visits only, free, about 90 minutes: daily June to September (Monday to Saturday 10:30 and 14:00, Sundays and holidays 11:00 and 15:00) from beneath the abbey's Torrione; groups of ten or more book ahead. The rest of the year on request (by phone, +39 055 862020). Times from 2026 reports; check before going.
trees.transport: A day trip from Florence: train from Santa Maria Novella to Pontassieve, then Autolinee Toscane bus 343 to Vallombrosa (45 to 60 minutes on the bus, about an hour and a quarter door to door; check the timetable).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, well above the neighbouring conifers, and by its long, straight, branchless lower trunk. It stands beside the path a short walk from the sequoia belvedere, on the guided route.
trees.pin_source: MASAF register point; the Commons photos carry exactly this coordinate, copied from the register rather than an independent fix at the trunk. iNaturalist has no usable observation within 100 m (obs 215460644, 2024, has 185 m accuracy).
trees.verify_notes: Alive: seen in Commons photos from 2019 and 2021 and described in a 2023 guided-visit report; no 2025/26 observation at this tree found (flag: recent alive evidence thin). Existence and species: MASAF 07/H222/FI/09 (515 cm, 51.5 m) plus Visit Tuscany, the Italian Botanical Heritage page, and Valdarno Post, which all name the Lambert pine as monumental in the arboreta. HEIGHT CONFLICT, keep all: register 51.5 m; Valdarno Post 2023 says 54 m with a girth of almost 8 m (a guide's spoken figure, implausible against the register 515 cm); Italian Botanical Heritage says over 131 ft (about 40 m) and a circumference of 19 ft (about 580 cm); Visit Tuscany gives the pine a nickname 'Nazareno' but the fetched page does not explain it (the reason is not recorded, do not invent one). A search summary quoting 47 m (Touring Club) was not seen on a page: do not use. Valdarno Post says the species holds the record for the second-largest cone in the world; Visit Tuscany notes visitors can see its cones. Pin approximate. No planting date for this specimen.

trees.name: The Holy Beech of Vallombrosa

location.address: Faggio Santo chapel, Circuito delle Cappelle, on the road to Secchieta, Vallombrosa, Reggello (FI)

trees.story:
The beech in this legend is long gone, and the tree standing in its place grew from it. Tradition says that in March 1036 Giovanni Gualberto, the founder of Vallombrosa, sheltered under an old beech on this slope, and the stone at the chapel beside it says the bare crown filled suddenly with leaves. Reggello's tourism office describes today's tree as a shoot born from that original plant about 150 years ago; a trail listing says closer to 120. Either way it is the heir, not the saint's own tree.

It is a big heir. The national register measures it at 3.8 metres round and 22 metres tall, at 1,032 metres above sea level, where it stands next to the small Cappella del Faggio Santo. A circular earthen bank was built round the site after 1636, with a dated inscription at its foot, so people were marking this spot long before the present trunk began.

Local lore adds that it is the first beech on the mountain to leaf in spring and the last to drop its leaves in autumn. Nobody has measured that, but late October is a good time to check. The chapel is a stop on the Circuito delle Cappelle, a walk of about 5.5 kilometres round the abbey, a few hundred metres up the road towards Secchieta.
trees.access: Free and open at all times, beside the surfaced road to Secchieta a few hundred metres from the abbey, next to a small chapel on the 5.5 km Circuito delle Cappelle. Mountain road; snow is possible in winter.
trees.transport: A day trip from Florence: train from Santa Maria Novella to Pontassieve, then Autolinee Toscane bus 343 to Vallombrosa (45 to 60 minutes on the bus; check the timetable). From the abbey it is a few hundred metres on foot along the road to Secchieta.

best_time.label: late October, when the beech turns copper and russet

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big beech, about 3.8 metres round, inside a circular earthen bank with a dated inscription at its foot. It stands beside the small Cappella del Faggio Santo on the road from the abbey towards Secchieta.
trees.pin_source: MASAF register point; the Commons photo 'Faggio secolare nel sito del Faggio Santo' carries exactly the same coordinate, copied from the register rather than an independent fix at the trunk.
trees.verify_notes: Existence: MASAF 05/H222/FI/09 (380 cm, 22 m, altitude 1032 m), Visit Tuscany (Reggello tourism: 'a shoot born from the original plant about 150 years ago', 380 cm, 22 m) and the Ecomuseo della Montagna Fiorentina page on the Faggio Santo; the chapel and legend are described by the FeelFlorence chapel-circuit page. AGE: Visit Tuscany says the tree is a shoot about 150 years old; a trail listing (not fetched, from a search summary) said about 120 years: treat as 120 to 150 and flag; the original beech of the legend is long gone. Alive: no dated 2025/26 observation found; a 2019 Commons photo shows a century-old beech at the site, the Chapel Circuit is a current tourist route. Register-only on vitality, hence flagged. Pin approximate (register point = Commons geotag).

trees.name: The Faggione of Prato a Marcaccio

location.address: Foresta di Sant'Antonio, Prato a Marcaccio, Reggello (FI), on trail R6 from Case di Sant'Antonio

trees.story:
This beech has a walk named after it. The metropolitan city of Florence publishes the Anello del Faggione, the ring of the big beech, a loop of about 5 kilometres through the Foresta di Sant'Antonio whose whole point is this one tree. Reggello's tourism office calls it probably the largest beech on the Pratomagno, the long ridge east of Florence.

It is not quite one tree. Two twin shoots grew together into a single trunk, which the national register measures at 5 metres round and 30 metres tall. One tourism page gives nearly 6 metres; the altitude is either 1,052 or 1,076 metres, depending on whose figure you read. It stands in a clearing called Prato a Marcaccio, inside a forest the comune of Reggello protects as a local nature area.

Nobody has published its age. If you know, tell us. The register kept it on its 2024 update, and a local mountain-walking group made it the goal of a day out in July 2016, but no recent photograph of it has surfaced, so a report from the trail would be welcome.

The walk leaves from Case di Sant'Antonio on trail R6, the Sentiero delle Fonticine, with about 150 metres of climb, an hour and a half to two hours in all. Getting to the trailhead realistically takes a car. It is up a forest road on the Reggello side of the mountain, around 40 kilometres from Florence.
trees.access: Free and open at all times on a public forest trail in the Foresta di Sant'Antonio. The Anello del Faggione (Itinerary 8a) is about 5 km with 150 m of climb, 1.5 to 2 hours. Mountain forest; snow is possible in winter.
trees.transport: Realistically by car or taxi: Case di Sant'Antonio is up a forest road on the Reggello side of the Pratomagno, around 40 km from Florence. By public transport, Vallombrosa (train to Pontassieve, bus 343) still leaves a long transfer.

best_time.label: October, when the beech forest turns copper and russet

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk made of two great shoots fused into one, about 5 metres round and 30 metres tall. It stands in the clearing of Prato a Marcaccio on the Anello del Faggione, the loop named after it.
trees.pin_source: MASAF register point only; no photograph geotag and no iNaturalist or OSM fix found. A trail named for the tree leads to it.
trees.verify_notes: Existence: MASAF 04/H222/FI/09 (500 cm, 30 m, altitude 1052 m) plus Visit Tuscany (Reggello tourism, photo credit Comune di Reggello Ufficio Ambiente: 'the Faggione stands thirty meters tall, trunk circumference of 5 meters, in the Forest of Sant'Antonio at an altitude of 1076'), plus the Citta Metropolitana di Firenze's own walking itinerary named for it (PDF; its text could not be extracted this pass, so only its title and the search description are relied on). Conflicts: girth 5 m (register, Visit Tuscany) vs nearly 6 m (a tourism page seen only in a search description); altitude 1052 vs 1076 m. Alive: no dated 2025/26 observation or photograph found; the only dated mention is a CAI Valdarno Superiore group outing on 2016-07-10 to the Faggione. It is presented as a current walk by the tourism pages and the register entry was in the 2024 ministerial update, so flagged 'register plus tourism pages, no recent sighting'. Pin approximate; no photo; Commons has nothing (the nearest file, an antler-shaped trunk 138 m away, is another tree). Distance from the Holy Beech pin is about 3 km straight line east (computed from coordinates); the road route is longer, treat as a separate stop reached by car.
